lesson.title: Spot a phishing message
lesson.subtitle: Five warning signs — and what to do next

video.title: Spot a phishing message
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Salma Haddad — secondary maths teacher (main character)
Dr Farah Rahman — university lecturer in education (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Staff room, end of the month. Salma sits with a cup of tea. Her phone buzzes: a text bubble of grey lines with an underlined link. She narrows her eyes, then raises one eyebrow at the camera.
scenes.animation: Phone buzz shake; text bubble slides up. Quick push-in on her raised eyebrow.
scenes.narration: “Your salary is on hold — confirm within twenty-four hours.” Hmm. My salary, on hold, by text message? Who writes like that?
scenes.sound: Phone buzz; light music bed starts.
scenes.vids: Character: illustrated secondary maths teacher, ink outlines. Show the message as grey lines plus a link shape; no readable bank or ministry names.

scenes.visual: Paper-grey card. The Darsi mark pops in, then the lesson title and the cyber track chip with its icon.
scenes.animation: Mark scales 0→100% with a small overshoot (≤ 200 ms); title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: how to spot a phishing message — and what to do when one arrives.
scenes.vids: Use the Darsi title template (see brand kit). Keep the chip as icon + word.

scenes.visual: A fishing line drops into a sea of message bubbles. On the hook: a bubble with a bank-building icon, then one with a school icon, then one with a gift box. A few fish-shaped phones swim close, curious.
scenes.animation: Hook swings gently; the bubble on it changes on each swing, 1 s apart.
scenes.narration: Phishing is a message that pretends to come from someone you trust — a bank, the ministry, even your head teacher — to trick you into clicking, paying or sharing a secret. It can come by text, email, chat apps or a phone call.
scenes.sound: Soft water plop as the hook drops.
scenes.vids: Simple flat sea and line. Keep the fish playful, not scary. No real logos on the bubbles.

scenes.visual: Salma’s message fills the screen. Five icons pop up around it one by one: clock, chain link, mask, key, gift box. Each connects to a part of the message with a short line.
scenes.animation: Icons pop 300 ms apart with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Look for five warning signs. Urgency or threats. A link or file you didn’t expect. A sender that doesn’t match. A request for your PIN, a one-time code or bank details. And a prize that’s too good to be true.
scenes.sound: A soft tick for each icon.
scenes.vids: Hold the five icons together for 3 seconds at the end so viewers can take them in.

scenes.visual: Clean card on white with the cyber track chip. A raised hand appears, then a phone with a call wave travelling to a saved-contact card with a check.
scenes.animation: Hand pops; the call wave travels left to right in 1 s.
scenes.narration: So here’s the habit. If a message pushes you to act fast, stop. Check through another channel — call the person on a number you already have, or open the official app yourself.
scenes.vids: Keep the card on screen for at least 6 seconds so teachers can read it in a second language.

scenes.visual: A school gate. A stranger holds out a hand and points toward the building. A teacher shakes her head kindly, then walks across the yard to the head teacher’s office door.
scenes.animation: Short walk cycle across the yard; the office door opens.
scenes.narration: It’s like a stranger at the school gate saying, “The head teacher sent me for the exam papers.” You wouldn’t hand them over. You’d walk to the office and ask. That walk is checking another way.
scenes.vids: Illustrated school gate and yard; no readable school names or signs.

scenes.visual: Dr Farah Rahman pops in at her university office, holding up her phone with a message bubble and a link shape. Three answer cards drop in: a finger tapping the link, a phone calling a bank-card icon, a reply bubble.
scenes.animation: Character slides in from the side; answer cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! A text says my bank card is blocked and gives a link to unlock it. What should I do first?
scenes.sound: Three gentle ‘pop’ sounds for the cards.
scenes.vids: The app pauses here (diamond marker). For the MP4 shared outside the app, hold this frame for 3 seconds with a small countdown ring.

scenes.visual: The ‘call the bank’ card gets a blue check badge. A bank card flips to show its back, and a call wave travels from the phone to the card.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops (150 ms). Quick 0.8 s confetti of three shapes in kola, sunbird and ink.
scenes.on_screen_text: Use the number on your card
scenes.narration: Call the bank on the number printed on your card — not the number in the message. A real problem will still be there after one phone call.
scenes.vids: Use blue for correct (never green) and always pair it with the check icon. Show no real bank names or card designs.

scenes.visual: Fast montage of four message cards, each with its warning icon: a clock on an exam-fee message; a key on a ‘sent by mistake’ call bubble; a gift box on a prize message; a document with a question mark from an unknown number.
scenes.animation: Each card flips in from the right, about 5 seconds each. Keep motion simple and readable on a small screen.
scenes.narration: Scams come in many shapes. “Pay the exam fee today or lose your place.” A caller who sent money “by mistake” and wants the code you just got. “You’ve won a laptop — just pay delivery.” A file called exam results from a number you don’t know.
scenes.vids: Use flat icons from the Darsi set on white cards. Do not show real app logos, bank names or brand names on screen.

scenes.visual: Salma taps a flag icon on the message, sends a short warning to the staff group, and the message slides into a bin. Then three panels: a browser page closing, an old key swapped for a new one, a phone calling a bank icon.
scenes.animation: Flag pops; message drops into the bin. Panels appear 300 ms apart.
scenes.narration: Spotted one? Report it with the app’s report button, warn your school, then delete it. Clicked by mistake? Don’t panic. Close the page. If you typed a password, change it now. If you shared bank details, call your bank straight away.
scenes.sound: Soft click, then a paper-crumple sound.
scenes.vids: Show a generic report flag, not a real app’s menu. Keep the three after-click panels on screen for at least 4 seconds.

scenes.visual: Salma holds up her phone: a chat bubble from a contact with a colleague’s photo asks for a code. Two answer cards bounce in: a warning triangle (scam) and a check mark (safe).
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. A colleague’s number writes: “I sent you a code by mistake — please forward it.” Scam or safe?
scenes.vids: Second diamond marker — the app pauses for the question. In the MP4, hold for 3 seconds, then highlight ‘scam’.

scenes.visual: The scam card gets the check badge. Then four summary cards line up: a warning triangle, a raised hand, a phone calling a saved contact, a flag beside a bin.
scenes.animation: Cards line up left to right, 250 ms apart.
scenes.narration: Scam — even from a friend’s number, because accounts get taken over. Remember: spot the sign, stop, check another way, then report and delete.
scenes.vids: Hold the four cards for 5 seconds.

scenes.visual: Salma’s classroom. Groups of pupils sort paper message cards into two piles on their desks; one pupil points to a gift-box doodle on a card and explains, others nod. End card: Darsi mark and ‘Next: Lock down your phone’.
scenes.animation: Cards slide into piles. End card fades in.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: write six short messages on paper. Pupils sort them into scam or safe — and point to the warning sign that gave each scam away.
scenes.sound: Music resolves; no end jingle longer than 1 s.
scenes.vids: Classroom: illustrated pupils in local school uniforms; avoid stereotyped imagery. End card from the Darsi template.

checkpoints.prompt: A text says your bank card is blocked and gives a link to unlock it. What’s the safest first step?

options.text: Tap the link to see what it says
Call the bank on the number on your card
Reply to ask if it’s real

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — the number on your card is one you can trust. Never use the link or number in the message.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — the link and the reply both go to whoever sent the message. Call the number on your card instead.

checkpoints.prompt: A colleague’s number asks you to forward a code sent to you “by mistake”. Scam or safe?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — accounts get taken over. A code sent to your phone is for you alone.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a colleague’s account can be taken over. Never forward a code; call them on their usual number.

video.vids_prompt: Create a 3 minute animated explainer video for teachers titled “Spot a phishing message”. Style: flat, friendly illustration with bold ink outlines, light grey backgrounds, a tangerine (#ff6a2b) brand colour and hibiscus pink (#f04a7e); no gradients or blur. Main character: Ms Salma Haddad, a secondary maths teacher. Follow the script scene by scene: a fake “salary on hold” text; what phishing is; five warning signs; stop and check through another channel; the school-gate analogy; examples of scams; how to report, delete and act after a click; two quiz pauses; end with a “scam or safe?” classroom sort. Use the narration exactly as written, a warm, calm voice, and keep on-screen text to six words or fewer per scene. No logos or brand names on screen.
